spec.title: Dry-run: a distributed token-bucket limiter
spec.intro: Build it in the order you would at a whiteboard: the algorithm alone first, then the part that makes it correct across many servers. Roughly 6 minutes if you talk while you type.

steps.title: State the shape before writing anything
steps.explain: Start by naming what you store per client. Two numbers is the whole state — that is the selling point of token bucket, and saying it up front tells the interviewer you know why you picked it.
steps.saysOutLoud: Per client I only need a token count and the time I last refilled. Everything else is derived.

steps.title: Refill lazily, never on a timer
steps.explain: A background timer per client would be thousands of timers. Instead compute how much time has passed and top up on access. This is the trick worth pointing out — it makes the algorithm O(1) memory and needs no scheduler.
steps.saysOutLoud: I refill lazily on read rather than running a timer per bucket.

steps.title: The single-node decision
steps.explain: Now the actual allow/deny. Note it returns the remaining count too — you need that for the response headers, and volunteering that detail shows you have shipped one of these.

steps.title: Now break it on purpose
steps.explain: Say plainly that the code above is wrong the moment there are two gateway nodes. Read-then-write across a shared store lets two nodes read the same 99 and both allow. Showing the bug before fixing it is what separates a memorised answer from a designed one.
steps.saysOutLoud: This is correct on one box and quietly wrong on ten — let me show the race.

steps.title: Redis holds the shared counter
steps.explain: This is a dependency you configure, not a component you build. What matters is naming the cost out loud: every request now takes a network round trip (~0.5–2 ms in-datacenter), and Redis becomes a hard dependency of every request your system serves.
steps.saysOutLoud: The counter has to be shared, so I'm accepting a round trip on every request and a new dependency.

steps.title: Make the check atomic with a Lua script
steps.explain: Redis runs a script atomically, so the read-modify-write of both fields happens with no interleaving. This is the standard production answer for token bucket and the thing to name explicitly — INCR alone can't do it because you need to update two fields together.

steps.title: Decide what happens when Redis is down
steps.explain: Interviewers listen for this. A limiter outage must not become an API outage — so fail open for general traffic. The exception is auth endpoints, where allowing unlimited attempts is worse than rejecting real users. Answer per endpoint class, not globally.
steps.saysOutLoud: Fail open, except on auth endpoints where I fail closed.

spec.closing: If asked to scale it further: batch by leasing 20 tokens at a time per node, which cuts round trips 20× and costs you a little over-admission. Name the trade rather than claiming exactness.
